subject: English
description: Direct ↔ reported speech conversion across tenses and moods

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'I am reading a book.'

options.option_text: He said that he was reading a book.
He said that he is reading a book.
He says that he was reading a book.
He told that I was reading a book.

questions.explanation: Reporting verb 'said' (past) shifts tense back: 'am reading' (present continuous) → 'was reading' (past continuous). Pronoun 'I' → 'he'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form of: She said, 'I will go tomorrow.'

options.option_text: She said that she would go tomorrow.
She said that she would go the next day.
She said that she will go the next day.
She said she is going tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Tense shift: will → would. Time expression shift: tomorrow → the next day / the following day. (Other shifts: today → that day; yesterday → the previous day; now → then; here → there; this → that.)

questions.stem: Indirect speech of: 'Please close the window,' the teacher said to the student.

options.option_text: The teacher said to close the window.
The teacher requested the student to close the window.
The teacher told that he should close the window.
The teacher ordered the student that please close the window.

questions.explanation: Polite imperatives (please/kindly) → 'requested'. Plain command → 'ordered / told'. The reporting structure: Verb + object + TO-infinitive. 'Please close' → 'requested ... to close'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form of: He said, 'The sun rises in the east.'

options.option_text: He said that the sun rose in the east.
He said that the sun rises in the east.
He said that the sun was rising in the east.
He says that the sun rises in the east.

questions.explanation: Universal truths / habitual facts / scientific laws DO NOT shift tense in indirect speech. Hence 'rises' stays 'rises'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form of: He asked her, 'Where do you live?'

options.option_text: He asked her where did she live.
He asked her where she lived.
He told her where she lived.
He asked where does she lives.

questions.explanation: Wh-questions in indirect speech: drop auxiliary 'do/does', turn into STATEMENT word-order (subject before verb). Tense shifts: do live → lived. 'asked her where she lived'. Reporting verb 'asked' — used for questions.

questions.stem: Indirect form of: 'Hurrah! We have won the match,' they said.

options.option_text: They said that they won the match.
They exclaimed joyfully that they had won the match.
They said hurrah, they won the match.
They told that we have won the match.

questions.explanation: Exclamatory direct sentences → use 'exclaimed' + adverb of emotion. 'Hurrah!' (joy) → 'exclaimed joyfully'. 'Alas!' → 'exclaimed sadly'. 'Bravo!' → 'applauded'. Tense: 'have won' → 'had won'.

questions.stem: Change to indirect: 'Let us go home,' she said.

options.option_text: She said to go home.
She suggested that they should go home.
She told to us go home.
She said let we go home.

questions.explanation: 'Let us' proposing joint action → reporting verb 'suggested' + 'should'. Structure: 'suggested that (subject) should (verb)'. 'Let us go' → 'suggested that they should go'.

questions.stem: She said to her mother, "I am feeling very tired now." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: She told her mother that she is feeling very tired then.
She told her mother that she was feeling very tired then.
She told her mother that she was feeling very tired now.
She told her mother that I was feeling very tired then.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'am' backshifts to 'was'; 'now' changes to 'then'; the first-person 'I' changes to 'she'. Option A fails to backshift 'is' to 'was'. Option C incorrectly retains 'now' — deictic time words must shift in indirect speech. Option D wrongly keeps the first-person pronoun 'I' instead of shifting to 'she'.

questions.stem: He told me that he had lost his keys the day before. Which of the following is the correct direct speech?

options.option_text: He said to me, "I have lost my keys yesterday."
He said to me, "I had lost my keys the day before."
He said to me, "I lost my keys yesterday."
He said to me, "I lose my keys yesterday."

questions.explanation: C is correct: past perfect 'had lost' in indirect reverses to simple past 'lost' in direct; 'the day before' converts back to 'yesterday'. Option A is wrong because present perfect cannot co-occur with 'yesterday' — a classic grammar trap. Option B wrongly retains the past perfect and the indirect time expression 'the day before', which belong only in reported speech. Option D uses simple present 'lose', which is grammatically wrong for a past event.

questions.stem: The priest said to the congregation, "May God bless you all!" Which of the following correctly reports this optative sentence in indirect speech?

options.option_text: The priest prayed that God may bless them all.
The priest wished that God might bless them all.
The priest said that God would bless them all.
The priest wished that God should bless them all.

questions.explanation: B is correct: optative sentences use the reporting verb 'wished/prayed'; the modal 'may' backshifts to 'might'; 'you' shifts to 'them'. Option A is wrong because 'may' is not backshifted to 'might' — a frequent error. Option C alters the meaning from a blessing/wish to a future prediction using 'would'. Option D inserts 'should', which carries obligation rather than optative force and is incorrect here.

questions.stem: He said, "If I were rich, I would travel the world." Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: He said that if he had been rich, he would have travelled the world.
He said that if he was rich, he would travel the world.
He said that if he were rich, he would travel the world.
He said that if he were rich, he will travel the world.

questions.explanation: C is correct: in a second conditional (counterfactual hypothesis), the subjunctive 'were' is preserved in indirect speech — hypothetical conditions do not undergo standard tense backshift. Option A wrongly converts the sentence to a third conditional (past perfect + would have), changing its meaning entirely. Option B replaces the subjunctive 'were' with indicative 'was', losing the counterfactual nuance. Option D incorrectly changes 'would' to 'will', which is not possible in a reported past-context sentence.

questions.stem: The interviewer asked the candidate, "Do you have any prior experience in this field?" Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: The interviewer asked whether he have any prior experience in that field.
The interviewer asked whether he had any prior experience in that field.
The interviewer asked that did he have any prior experience in that field.
The interviewer asked if he has had any prior experience in this field.

questions.explanation: B is correct: yes/no questions convert using 'whether/if'; the auxiliary 'do' is dropped and 'have' backshifts to 'had'; 'you' shifts to 'he'; 'this' shifts to 'that'. Option A omits the required backshift of 'have' to 'had'. Option C wrongly retains question-word inversion ('did he have') after 'that' — indirect questions always use affirmative word order. Option D uses the present perfect 'has had' instead of simple past 'had', and retains 'this' instead of changing it to 'that'.

questions.stem: "I have been working here since morning and I may finish by evening," he said. Which of the following is the correct indirect speech?

options.option_text: He said he had been working there since morning and might finish by evening.
He said he has been working here since morning and may finish by evening.
He said he had been working there from morning and would finish by evening.
He said he had been working here since morning and might finish by evening.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'have been working' backshifts to 'had been working'; 'here' shifts to 'there' (place deixis); 'may' backshifts to 'might'; 'since' is retained because it marks the start of a period, not a deictic reference. Option B makes no changes to tense, place, or modal — a complete failure to report. Option C wrongly replaces 'since' with 'from' (altering the grammatical structure) and uses 'would' instead of 'might', which changes probability to prediction. Option D correctly backshifts tense and modal but fails to change 'here' to 'there' — a subtle place-deixis error many students miss.

questions.stem: My friend said to me, "Your brother told me that you had promised to help him." Which of the following correctly converts this to indirect speech?

options.option_text: My friend told me that my brother had told him that I had promised to help him.
My friend told me that my brother told him that I promised to help him.
My friend told me that his brother had told him that I had promised to help me.
My friend told me that his brother had told him that I had promised to help him.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Your brother' (the friend addressing the narrator) → 'my brother' (narrator's brother in indirect); 'told me' (the friend was told) → 'had told him' (backshift + pronoun shift); 'you had promised' → 'I had promised'; 'him' (the brother) remains 'him'. Option B omits backshift of both 'told' and 'promised'. Options C and D both use 'his brother' — but 'his' would incorrectly refer to the friend's own brother; the original 'your brother' referred to the narrator's brother, so 'my brother' is the only correct rendering. Option C additionally uses 'help me' instead of 'help him', swapping the object incorrectly.
